title: Grief Class 4
speaker: Reizan Bob Penny
summary: The talk emphasizes that healing from grief and finding hope for the future requires acknowledging our interconnectedness with others and the world around us. Rather than isolating ourselves or focusing solely on individual emotional pain, we need to address the collective suffering of humanity and the Earth as a whole. This involves recognizing the global nature of our problems, such as climate change, and working together towards a more compassionate and wise future.

sentences.text: Well, welcome.
It's our last class.
In this class we're moving outward in circles, contemplating maybe a more global perspective on grief, but still staying in touch with ourselves and our own process in that.
What we've seen so far is that grieving is a process of moving forward in time.
We've lost someone or something has come to an end, yet we move on.
The tension between our movement and what is left behind is one way to measure our grief.
And we've seen that when our grief is unresolved, we experience blindness towards how we move forward and also blindness to how we imagine our future.
This idea of blindness to the future can have serious implications for continued suffering.
In exploring grief, we can easily make a connection between our own feelings and the wider world around us.
Being around someone who is depressed is depressing.
Being around someone compassionate and energetic enlivens our sense of care and lifts us up.

Although the paradigm of modern psychology predominantly places the individual in isolation, alone in the contemplation of their past and the scars suffered there that may have added to their own personal story, the self exists actually as a self in relation.
The ego develops in affiliation with others and the wider world, and healing similarly occurs within these wider connections.
What we most often need in our healing process is to be heard, accepted and understood, to see that we are not alone.
Miriam Greenspan, in the book we've been using in our class, has much to say about this, and also about a division between the personality types of the bystander and the carrier, as she calls them.
The carrier is the one who individually exhibits feelings about some situation.
Frequently, a therapist will identify that the one coming in for therapy is simply the one who is not alone.

Frequently, a therapist will identify that the one coming in for therapy is simply the lightning rod, the carrier, the one who is exhibiting emotions for a whole family system which is in emotional crisis.
The bystander, although equally part of the situation, adopts the role of not feeling, usually manifested as keeping your wits about you, being in control or being objective.
These attributes are more highly valued in a predominantly patriarchal culture, what Greenspan calls a bystander culture.

Social bystanding, standing aside or exhibiting numb or even overwhelmed indifference in the face of injustice, lends credibility to the injustice, and a destructive cycle is perpetuated into the future.

Another way of looking at all this is to see our world as one family, where the nations are individuals, each exhibiting various roles within the family: the bully, the appeaser, the denier, the aggressor, the healer, the black sheep, etc.
Looking at it this way, we can see that our world family exhibits a good level of dysfunction.
One of the greatest dysfunctional aspects of recent humanity has been its relationship to the natural world.
I should really say lack of relationship, because the problem goes right down to basic principles.
Nature has been relegated to a sub-status in all our considerations.
We are just beginning to experience some level of discomfort when we speak of natural resources as if nature existed only for our use.
But our best recent attempts to work in sustainable patterns are as yet a wholly undefined philosophy.
The real root of the sustainability ethos goes back to the Hindu concept of ahimsa, doing the least harm.
But we haven't yet fully moved into that understanding, and so our movements towards sustainability remain tinged with a human-centered stain.
Nature has not yet gained an equal status within the community of societies in the human world family.
Until that happens, we will never have real sustainability.
So how do we get some handle on how we are doing in healing our world?

To go forward with healing beyond ourselves as isolated individuals, we need to be open to the suffering and grief manifested in wars, social and cultural divisions, the destruction of whole species, and perhaps irreparable changes we, through our actions, are bringing to the natural world.
Our grief is tied to all of this in ways still to be understood, but the connection is certainly there.
Greenspan presents a set of questions concerning this, but claims to not yet have the answers.
They are: How are our personal dark emotions related to a worldwide context of collective violence and environmental destruction?
How do we begin to understand mass psychology in an age of global distress and terror?
How must we change ourselves in order to meet the challenges of global crisis in the 21st century?
And how do we address the need for healing of the human family and the Earth rather than just the individual?

One observation I've engaged with at different times for many years is to notice what's happening in the popular culture as a way to gauge how we collectively, as a society, are viewing or perhaps not choosing to view the future we are setting up for ourselves through our collective actions.
It seems that how we view the future is directly related to how well we've healed our past.

I tend to view what we refer to as the popular culture, entertainment, music, movies, as literally the contemporary substitute for the functions that in ancient societies were addressed by storytelling, song, and myth.

In those older cultures, these forms drew from deep sources and archetypes, and therefore presented to those in the present old and established values towards time, change, birth, death, and all the most important issues of life.
In our very secular modern society, popular culture seems to be always, through art, dipping back into these same archetypes to achieve a similar kind of referencing for us today.
But without the traditional grounding that older forms of entertainment possessed, today's efforts wax and wane in their focus.

I've noticed this fluctuation of focus especially in how movies relate to the future, especially the near future, the near future that we ourselves right now are spending our lives setting up through our collective actions to take place.
And yet, curiously, whole periods of time will go by when, judging from the output of movies each year, one might assume that literally no future exists within our collective conception.

Movies of the 40s and 50s focused on the present, or the very recent and compelling past of the great wars, or former historical times, or, in the emerging genre of science fiction, phantasmagorical visions of a distant future, a much more technological future.
Think Buck Rogers or Barbarella.
In some ways, these movies anticipated the conceptual processes necessary to invent the new technologies of the future.
On Star Trek, Kirk's communicator was nothing more than a powerful cell phone, which at the time seemed almost like an unimaginable device.
And the current generation of small handheld computers, such as iPhones and notepads, are only beginning to approach the almost magical properties of Spock's tricorder.
But it was perhaps the movie 2001: A Space Odyssey where the existential alienation of humanity in a future technological world was first best depicted.

Here we're humans, still essentially not far advanced from our ancestral evolutionary beginnings, but having lives completely enmeshed with a now totally technologically constructed environment, feeling the same old emotions humans have always felt, but now without ability to reference those emotions back to a source in nature.
Songs of technological alienation, such as David Bowie's Space Oddity or Elton John's Rocket Man, found ready and understanding audiences.
Bowie also created a song inspired directly from the science fiction of Aldous Huxley and gave it the same title, 1984.

My attention towards these sorts of trends in movies and such became focused in the late 70s, as the year 1984 loomed on the not so distant horizon, and the social discourse related to the future of the natural environment was, similarly to now, taking off.

One can go back and find a bewildering number of titles published in the 70s concerning future environmental trends, then hardly any such books for two decades until shortly after the year 2000, and now a new explosion of focus in that direction.
And as for movies, there were either movies about the past, the present, or the distant future.
Star Trek was set in the 23rd century, I believe. 2001 stood as the only offering of a vision of the near future.
In fact, Kubrick's choice of the year 2001 is significant.
In any discussions of the near future during the late 70s, there was an amazing blank space.
No one, not movie makers or even politicians, discussed anything about the future beyond maybe 1984.

The specter of Huxley's vision hung heavy over that date, much more so than the current specter being built up for the end of the Mayan calendar in 2012, arguably a more tangible date, based on age-old calculations, something we might have at least some curiosity, if not outright concern about.
But beyond 1984, the only other reference date for the near future thrown around was always, and always referred to in this way, the year 2000.
By the year 2000, we would all be living like the Jetsons.
By the year 2000, environmental degradation of some form or another would be at this or that level.
By the year 2000, we would have achieved general eradication of racism, sexism, pollution, and all manner of injustice.
By the year 2000, we will have, by our mutual and collective ignorance, blown all the people and cities on the planet to smithereens many, many times over.

This last image was, of course, the pervasive one, although perhaps the least elucidated and explored in books or movies: nuclear Armageddon, fulfillment of prophecies of biblical proportion, would be achieved, certainly, by the year 2000, and not by an intercession of angels or devils, but by our own hands.

Our collective and somewhat understandable reluctance to look at this potential future directly for what it certainly could easily be lent itself to this general absence of any imagery for the near future.
Kubrick, again, is almost the sole visionary for all of us, with movies like the future social decadence of A Clockwork Orange and the blackest intertwining of comedy and tragedy in Dr.
Strangelove.

The power of these visions was that they presented something truly approachable, a depiction of the near future that, by simple, reasonable extrapolation, we could easily imagine actually happening based upon the lives we currently were living.
The year 2000, still a quarter century in the future, was held up abstractly as a catchall for whatever hope or dread we held for the future.
It was far enough away that anything we said about it we all knew could as easily end up being true or false.
Nothing was said about the intervening years, so there was never laid down a trajectory or pathway to achieve any end.
Doomsday books of the environmental movement like Barry Commoner's The Closing Circle were fringe information and given almost no voice in the greater discourse.
The basic fact was that collectively humanity held up little hope of reaching the year 2000.
Most of us, somewhere in a deeply shared emotional space, believed we would all be blown up by then.
By the late 80s and the 90s, our cultural production of imagery and stories shrunk even more, and any focus on the impending threshold of destruction was increasingly ignored.
The fall of the Berlin Wall gave enough collective psychic relief that we all felt we could let go of a great deal of our dread, even though many conditions had not really changed.
The epidemic of the sequel had descended into our societal image-making.

Star Trek, versions one through seven or eight, spun forward through some fantasy time frame as nothing more than a continuing soap opera, with a cast of lovable characters playing out mini-plays on various social themes.
The message was, even in the distant future, we will still be struggling with racism, sexism and environmental destruction.
Hardly a vision that laid out a path forward.
Star Wars was essentially the Knights of the Round Table in spaceships, a morality play of good versus evil, but too abstract again to suggest a real path forward.
And the comedy sequel, Back to the Future, saw a perpetually chipper and youthful Michael J.
Fox always end up with a girl and back safe and sound in his cozy all-American hometown.
As the actual transition of the year 2000 approached to within an easily comprehensible near future of its own, almost nothing was said anymore about the year 2000.
And then, with the whimper of the fuss over Y2K, the barrier was leapt over with almost no consequence.

Without a doubt, it's now clear that a sort of collective grief, manifested as almost paralyzed hand-wringing, hung over our planetary society for the last half of the 20th century: grief and associated shame remembered for Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and also grief in anticipation of the nuclear midnight represented by that clock, the union of concerned scientists that marked our time left on Earth.
Like Scrooge, we were collectively living within a Dickensian tale.
We struggled through a long night, being led to one and then another horrible contemplation of what, with our own making, were our potential futures, never wanting to look.
Growing up, I probably felt this intuitively, loving the macabre theatre of Halloween and all that it offered to bring forth hidden truths.
I repeatedly, for a number of years consecutively, dressed on All Hallows' Eve as the specter of death, scythe on shoulder, grimly silent, one snaggled finger pointing to the future.
And yet we simply ignored it all and partied forward.
Now we even say to party like it's 1990, meaning with blindfolds securely fastened.
Then of course came September 11th.
Was this now a new and different world?
In the sense that many meant, I never felt that way.

I've always felt that September 11th showed us far more about our pre-existing blindness, our arrogance in the face of suffering and our emotional isolation from each other than it did with revealing some age of new danger requiring our stepped-up vigilance.
Along with this event has come something equally profound in the social psyche, but this time not an event discernible in time or even known to conclusively exist: global climate change.

As we've gotten beyond the initial shock and awe of September 11th and settled into a numb acceptance of what seems to be perpetual war, our sense of urgency concerning the war on terror has scabbed over, creating a permanent disfiguring scar in our psyche where normal movements of compassion and altruism feel forever impeded by the deep pain of an old wound, so that we just can't ever let our guard down.
But now the awareness of climate change has been raised to an equal status with all this, and again the experts are dueling it out.
All these problems can be solved, we are told with great assurance by our leaders, if we maintain ever-increasing vigilance, ever-increasing technological advancement, ever-increasing determination.
But never are we encouraged to go into how we feel.

And yet all this suffering and these potential calamities have only one real solution, and that is if we learn finally to turn to each other and resolve our pain and wounds collectively and with nature.

Only then will the needed energy and resolve flow forward to relieve the suffering of many and free up the focus of leaders and societies to make the needed course corrections we so desperately need to make.
And yet I have some reasons for hope for the future.

I see glimmers of recognition in the popular culture, recognizing new and healing ways forward, in a whole explosion of movies dealing with the very near future, but based upon a future fully imaginable, stemming from current events.

Nothing like Kubrick, of course, and not all positive, but there are many new movies about a near future world changed, both for good and bad, through pandemic, through war, through environmental implosion.
Perhaps our focus is beginning to shift.

An encouraging sign is that books contemplating the future of the natural environment, in contrast to books from the 70s which spoke mostly of threatening trends and hypotheses of impending catastrophe, now speak much more towards how we can actively create something more positive going forward.
Whether we have the exact facts lined up, whether the experts are figuring all right or not, is not the real issue.
The real advancement is that we are finally and collectively beginning to look with much wider and clearer eyes at the future.
Each of us individually therefore has a vital role to play.

Being in touch with our connected feelings, about our own personal [unclear: "greases"] and losses, about the suffering of people and the planet, will be the new skill so necessary for everyone to gain competence in.
Luckily for us as Buddhists, it's what we've been doing already.
A recognition of Buddhism's ability to provide just this sort of focus is, I believe, what is at the heart of the new popularization of Buddhism within the dominant culture.
The first thing to do is look around us and recognize what is going on and where we are headed.
Here we can see that a crucial shift to awareness has already begun to happen.
In the distant future, this shift, and not the winning or losing of a military battle, will be hailed as the true turning point of the world.
Global warming is fully on the table.
The tide has shifted, and those who disbelieve this are waning.
As a little more time goes forward, this shift will solidify.
But it will probably be that it will take some soon-to-be event, some natural disaster that can only be explained by climate change and nothing else, to make the shift complete.
Let's hope this event is not too catastrophic.
But certainly our collective blindness will not be washed away until something like this presents itself.
It is simply the nature of humanity to not want to see until there is no other choice.

Whether this happens in time for us to do anything about any inevitable future will be almost beside the point, because whether we see or admit what the future, by obvious evidence in the present, holds, will not change the future from coming.
One notion going around right now is that we have the ability, like some sort of grand technical wizards, to literally change the course of nature on a dime.
Well, certainly we will finally make some drastic course corrections and will mitigate the effects of climate change.
And certainly humanity will have to go through some very drastic revisions of how it does its business on the planet.
But the real shift will be that we are now firmly and squarely imagining the future through eyes of compassion and wisdom.
So, thinking about that, I thought that what we would do is break up into pairs.
The critical part of this little exercise today is to try and speak to these questions from our feelings, and not what we think about the future, but what we feel when we contemplate the future.
What feelings are in there as we look out at something we maybe don't usually choose to look at?
What do we feel about the continued threat of nuclear war?
How have we felt about that in the past?
Are our feelings different now than they were 20 years ago?
How do we feel about the state of the country 20 years ago?
How do we feel about the state of the planet and the natural world and where it's headed?
Remember, not what we think about where it's headed, but how do we feel when we contemplate looking out into the future, at the natural world and what direction it seems to be going in?
Do we feel anxious?
Do we feel sadness?
Some sense of optimism?
Do we feel about the world younger people will inherit when we're gone?
What's it going to be like?
How do we feel about that?
How do we feel about the kind of place it might be then?
So this is all by way of practicing what is, I think, going to be an essential practice in this century, that people have positive, clear focus on the future.
They have some sense of awareness of the collective feelings that everyone holds towards the future.
